notwithstanding: Despite; even if something else says otherwise.
hereinafter: From this point on in the document.
mutatis mutandis: Apply the same rule, changing only what must change.
save as otherwise provided: Unless another rule says something different.
shall be deemed: The law treats it as true even if it is not literally so.
prima facie: On first look, before full examination.
ex parte: Decided in the absence of the other party.
suo motu: On its own initiative, without a petition.
ultra vires: Beyond the legal power of the person or body.
locus standi: The right to bring a case to court.
indemnify: Promise to cover someone else's losses or costs.
indemnity: A promise to make good another person's loss.
jointly and severally: Each person can be made to pay the whole amount.
liquidated damages: A pre-agreed amount payable on breach (Section 74, Contract Act).
force majeure: Events beyond control, like floods or war, that excuse performance.
lessor: The owner who gives property on lease.
lessee: The person who takes property on lease.
licensor: The owner who allows use of property.
licensee: The person allowed to use property.
encumbrance: A charge, loan or claim attached to property.
hypothecation: Using movable property as loan security while keeping it.
lien: right to hold property until paid
A right to keep someone's property until a debt is paid.
covenant: A formal promise in a deed.
severability: If one clause is invalid, the others still apply.
arbitration: Settling a dispute through a private arbitrator instead of a court.
jurisdiction: Which court has the power to hear a case.
cognizable: An offence where police can register an FIR and arrest without a warrant.
non-cognizable: An offence where police need a magistrate's order to investigate.
cognizance: When a court formally takes notice of an offence to begin proceedings.
bailable: An offence where bail is a matter of right.
non-bailable: An offence where bail depends on the court.
compoundable: An offence the victim can settle with the accused.
anticipatory bail: Bail granted before arrest to someone who fears arrest.
surety: A person who guarantees that the accused will appear in court.
remand: Sending an accused to police or judicial custody.
acquittal: A court decision that the accused is not guilty.
conviction: A court decision that the accused is guilty.
charge sheet: The police report filed after investigation listing the accusations.
affidavit: A written statement sworn to be true.
injunction: court order to do or stop something
A court order requiring someone to do or not do an act.
decree: The formal result of a civil case.
plaintiff: person who files a civil case
The person who brings a civil suit.
defendant: The person against whom a civil suit is filed.
appellant: The person who files an appeal.
respondent: The person who answers an appeal or petition.
petitioner: The person who files a petition.
vakalatnama: The document authorising a lawyer to act for you.
caveat: A notice asking the court not to pass orders without hearing you.
tort: A civil wrong, other than breach of contract, causing harm.
estoppel: can't go back on your word
A rule stopping someone from denying what they earlier said or did.
easement: A right to use someone else's land, like a pathway.
consideration: What each party gives or promises in exchange.
void: Having no legal effect from the start.
voidable: Valid until the affected party chooses to cancel it.
testator: The person who makes a will.
power of attorney: A document letting someone act on your behalf.
lock-in period: A period during which you cannot end the agreement without penalty.
stamp duty: A tax paid to make certain documents legally valid.
inter se: Between or among the parties themselves.
ipso facto: By that very fact or act.
status quo: The situation as it is now.
